title: Local services - overview
description: Resources, requests, traces, service metrics and logs for the local kind cluster, one row per signal. The CPU and Memory rows are profiler-reported, so only services running a profiler appear there and sampled heap is not the pod's resident memory - the Container resources row is.

list.name: service
list.label: Service (CPU, memory, traces)
list.description: Pyroscope's own service_name label, read live from the datasource. Drives the At a glance, CPU, Memory, Requests and Profiles rows. It does not reach the Container memory or scraped-metrics panels, which are keyed by pod and by the Kubernetes app label.

list.name: logservice
list.label: Log stream (logs)
list.description: Loki's service_name label, which is not the same thing as the Service picker. Alloy sets it from each log line's own `service` field and falls back to the pod's `app` label when a line has none, so one service can appear twice under two spellings, and services that never profile appear here too. Drives the Logs row only.

list.name: exclude
list.label: Exclude streams (logs)
list.description: Streams dropped from every Logs panel, as one regex. Matches whole names, so `kube-.*` covers every kube component and a new Gen3 service is kept without editing this. To hide one more service add `|its-name`; to see everything, clear the box. A stream excluded here shows nothing even when picked in Log stream.

list.name: logfilter
list.label: Log filters (logs)
list.description: Ad hoc label filters appended to every Loki query on the board. Add them by clicking a field in a log line's details, or with the + here.

panels.title: CPU now
panels.description: Latest CPU the profiler attributed to each service. 0.02 cores means 2% of one core - CPU-seconds consumed per second of wall clock, the same unit as a Kubernetes CPU request or limit, where 100m is 0.1 cores.

panels.title: Heap in use now
panels.description: Latest sampled heap in use: the bytes the profiler saw allocated and still live. It is not what the kernel charges the container, which also covers the runtime itself, its shared libraries, buffers allocated inside C extensions, and memory the allocator has freed but kept back from the OS - for the Python services profiled here that is CPython's allocator, and a Go service would instead hold the runtime's stacks and spans. Expect an order of magnitude between the two figures. Read the Container memory row for what a limit is enforced against, and this panel for which code is holding objects.

panels.title: CPU by service
panels.description: CPU as sampled by the profiler. 0.02 cores means 2% of one core - CPU-seconds consumed per second of wall clock, the same unit as a Kubernetes CPU request or limit, where 100m is 0.1 cores. It covers the process the profiler is attached to, so it is not the container's total.

panels.title: CPU by pod
panels.description: One series per replica. 0.02 cores means 2% of one core - CPU-seconds consumed per second of wall clock, the same unit as a Kubernetes CPU request or limit, where 100m is 0.1 cores. Pods that have been replaced keep their series for as long as their profiles sit inside the time range.

panels.title: Allocation rate
panels.description: Bytes allocated per second, including memory freed again immediately. High here with a flat heap in use is churn, not a leak.

panels.title: Heap in use
panels.description: Bytes the profiler sampled as allocated and still live - what the program itself is holding. Read it for which code holds objects and whether that is growing. For what the kernel charges the container, which is what a limit is enforced against, see the Container memory row.

panels.title: Objects in use
panels.description: The count of live sampled allocations, where Heap in use is their bytes. Bytes flat while objects climb means many small objects accumulating; bytes divided by objects gives the average object size.

panels.title: Container memory (working set) by pod
panels.description: Working set as the kernel accounts it: pages charged to the container's cgroup, minus the page cache it could reclaim under pressure. This is the number Kubernetes evicts and OOM-kills on, so it decides whether the pod lives - but it counts memory the process is not using, including the interpreter, shared libraries and anything its allocator has held back from the OS. The profiler rows above count what the program allocated and still holds. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions, and the gap between them is the runtime's overhead. Dashed lines are each container's limit; a container without one has no line, because cAdvisor reports its limit as 0 rather than leaving the series out. Not filtered by the Service picker: these series are keyed by pod and container.

panels.title: OOM kills
panels.description: Out-of-memory kills counted by the kernel. Flat at zero until something is killed, which is the point: a container that vanished mid-request with nothing in its own logs shows up here and nowhere else. Read it beside the memory table - a pod killed at its limit was at 100% there a moment earlier. Not filtered by the Service picker: these series are keyed by pod and container, which carry neither spelling of the name the picker holds.

panels.title: Memory used vs limit
panels.description: Working set now, the pod's total limit, and the ratio. Pods whose containers declare no memory limit read `none` and `no limit` rather than being dropped or shown at zero - cAdvisor reports their limit as 0, and there is nothing for a percentage to be of. Values are summed over the pod's containers, so a sidecar counts toward both columns. Not filtered by the Service picker: these series are keyed by pod, which carries neither spelling of the name the picker holds.

panels.title: Container CPU by pod
panels.description: CPU the container actually consumed, from cAdvisor - the counterpart to the profiler's CPU row above, and the pair that shows how much CPU the profiler never sees. 0.02 cores means 2% of one core. Not filtered by the Service picker: these series are keyed by pod and container, which carry neither spelling of the name the picker holds.

panels.title: CPU used vs limit
panels.description: Consumption as a share of the container's own CPU limit. Only containers that declare a limit appear; the rest are absent rather than shown at zero, since there is nothing to be a share of. Check this panel before reading CPU throttling: a flat zero there means headroom if a limit exists here, and nothing at all if it does not. Not filtered by the Service picker: these series are keyed by pod and container.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!="", namespace=~"default|monitoring"}[$__rate_interval])) / (sum by (pod) (container_spec_cpu_quota{container!="", namespace=~"default|monitoring"} / container_spec_cpu_period{container!="", namespace=~"default|monitoring"}) > 0)

panels.title: CPU throttling
panels.description: The share of scheduling periods in which the kernel stopped the container after it spent its quota. Only a container with a CPU limit can throttle, so a flat zero here means either headroom or no limit - check CPU used vs limit to tell which. This is the usual reason a service is slow while its own CPU graph looks unremarkable. Not filtered by the Service picker: these series are keyed by pod and container, which carry neither spelling of the name the picker holds.

panels.title: Request rate by endpoint
panels.description: Inbound server spans per second, by route template. Derived by Tempo's metrics generator from the spans it receives, not exported by the service. The series exist only while traces arrive, so a quiet service leaves a gap rather than a zero.

panels.title: Latency p95 by endpoint
panels.description: 95th percentile of inbound server span duration. The marks are exemplars: individual requests carrying their trace ID, so a spike can be opened as the trace that caused it. Derived by Tempo's metrics generator from the spans it receives, not exported by the service, so the series exist only while traces arrive and a quiet service leaves a gap rather than a zero.

panels.title: Latency heatmap
panels.description: The full distribution of inbound span duration, not just its 95th percentile: two bands rather than one is the shape a p95 line hides, typically a fast path and a slow one. The magenta marks are exemplars - each one is a real request that landed in that cell, carrying its trace ID, so a hot spot can be opened as a trace rather than guessed at. Hovering names the service and span; clicking follows it to Tempo. Buckets and exemplars both come from Tempo's metrics generator, so they exist only while traces arrive.

panels.title: Slowest endpoints
panels.description: p95 per route across the whole time range shown, ranked, so the worst endpoint names itself instead of being picked out of a crowded legend. It reads the range rather than a rate interval on purpose: a p95 over the last few minutes is empty whenever traffic is not arriving right now. Routes with no samples in the range are dropped rather than listed blank. Server spans only.

targets.expr: topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (service, span_name, le) (rate(traces_spanmetrics_latency_bucket{service=~"${service:pipe}", span_kind="SPAN_KIND_SERVER"}[$__range]))) > 0)

panels.title: Error rate by span
panels.description: Spans whose status is ERROR, of every kind - not just endpoints. A server span is a request that failed, a client span is a call this service made that failed, and an internal span is a step inside it, which is how a failure that propagates up a call chain shows as several series at once. Empty until a span actually carries that status: a handled 500 that never marks its span is invisible here. Derived by Tempo's metrics generator from the spans it receives, not exported by the service, so the series exist only while traces arrive.

panels.title: Recent traces
panels.description: Newest traces for the selected services. Click a Trace ID to open it in Tempo; its logs link resolves through Loki's trace_id metadata.

panels.title: Service graph
panels.description: Who calls whom, derived by Tempo from span pairs rather than declared anywhere. Nodes are not all services: a datastore appears as its own node, and `user` is a request that arrived with no parent span, meaning anything entering from outside. Grafana draws those two with a dashed outline because Tempo marks them un-instrumented, which is the only labelling the panel supports - the Service dependencies table beside it names each edge in words. Edges carry request rate and latency, so an N+1 query pattern shows here before it shows in CPU. Needs traffic, and ignores both pickers.

panels.title: Service dependencies
panels.description: The same edges the graph draws, named. Kind is Tempo's `connection_type`: a blank one is service to service, `database` is a datastore the client queried, and `virtual_node` is not a caller at all but a request that arrived with no parent span - anything entering from outside the traced system. The graph cannot say this in text: its node subtitle is reserved for the service namespace, and its only marker for a non-service node is a dashed outline. Database names come from the span's database attributes, which for these charts is the `<chart>_<release>` name the chart generates, so a service and its own database can appear under two different spellings.

panels.title: Request rate by status (all services)
panels.description: Counted by the service itself through cdispyutils request_metrics and read from its /metrics, so it is independent of the trace pipeline and survives a service that never exports a span. Selected by metric name (`.+_api_requests_total`) rather than by service, so anything using that helper appears without editing this dashboard. That panel ignores the Service picker, which is why the title says so: its series carry `app`, from Kubernetes. The Kubernetes `app` label and the name a service registers with the SDK need not match - hyphen against underscore is the usual difference - and no variable format converts one into the other.

panels.title: CPU by endpoint
panels.description: CPU attributed to the route that was executing when each sample was taken, which is the one thing the flame graphs below cannot tell you at a glance: they merge every request together. Only samples taken inside a span carry span_name, so background work and startup are absent here while still appearing in CPU by service.

panels.title: CPU profile
panels.description: Merged across every service selected in the Service picker. Pick a single service to read it. The totals are summed over the dashboard's time range, so they grow as the range widens rather than describing a moment.

panels.title: Heap in use profile
panels.description: Merged across every service selected in the Service picker. Pick a single service to read it. The totals are summed over the dashboard's time range, so they grow as the range widens rather than describing a moment.

panels.title: Log volume by service
panels.description: Lines per second per stream, driven by the Log stream picker rather than by Service. Alloy takes `service_name` from each line's own `service` field and falls back to the pod's `app` label when a line has none, so one service can own two streams under two spellings, and services that never profile appear here too. The Kubernetes `app` label and the name a service registers with the SDK need not match - hyphen against underscore is the usual difference - and no variable format converts one into the other.

panels.title: Log volume by level
panels.description: `detected_level` is inferred by Loki per line, not a label the service sets, so `unknown` means it could not find one rather than that the line was unimportant.

panels.title: Error rate by service
panels.description: Error lines per second per service, which for much of this cluster is the only error signal there is: a service that serves no metrics and exports no spans still logs. Driven by the Log stream and Exclude controls, and by the level Loki inferred - a service logging severity in a shape Loki cannot parse is invisible here.

panels.title: Recent logs
panels.description: Oldest first, so the newest line is at the bottom and the panel opens scrolled to it. Each line is prefixed with its service. The prefix is added by the query with `line_format`, because the panel's displayed-fields option replaces the log line rather than prefixing it - so a copied line carries the prefix too, and Prettify JSON no longer applies to lines that were pure JSON. Level filtering, search, wrapping and sort live in the panel's own controls on the right. Clicking a field in a line's details adds it to the Log filters control at the top, which narrows every Loki panel. Lines carrying `trace_id` link to the trace in Tempo.

panels.title: Errors and warnings
panels.description: The same lines and the same service prefix, filtered to the level Loki inferred - so a service logging its own severity in a format Loki cannot read is missing here even while it fails. Search and the display toggles are in the panel's controls; the level filter there narrows this further rather than widening it, since the query is already fixed to error and warn.
